name: Poly-L-lactic acid (Sculptra)

lead: Sculptra is a Galderma injectable whose active ingredient is poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), a biodegradable synthetic polymer [1][4]. Unlike hyaluronic acid fillers, which add immediate volume, PLLA is classed as a collagen biostimulator: it is injected to prompt the body to lay down collagen gradually, restoring facial volume and smoothing wrinkles over time [1][4].

It was first approved by the US FDA in 2004 for facial fat loss in people with HIV, and its indications later expanded to nasolabial folds and cheek wrinkles, according to Grokipedia [1]. Systematic reviews of randomized trials report improved skin elasticity, wrinkle reduction and facial volume, with effects sustained for up to 25 months [2][3].

paras: PLLA microparticles are described as promoting a subclinical inflammatory response that leads to collagen deposition in the extracellular matrix, so volume is restored gradually rather than immediately [4]. A 2025 gene analysis in a randomized comparison reported that PLLA triggered regeneration-related gene activity, whereas calcium hydroxylapatite induced inflammation-related activity [7].

Reported adverse events across trials are mostly mild to moderate: bruising, hematoma, tenderness, nodules and swelling [3]. A 2026 systematic review found mild injection-site pain and swelling as the most frequent effects and reported at least one serious case [2]. It is injected by trained clinicians. Poor technique or product selection can cause lumps, which reviewers list among the main adverse events [3].

lead: Sculptra is a brand of injectable poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), a synthetic, biocompatible and biodegradable polymer, marketed by Galderma as a collagen-stimulating dermal treatment [1][2]. It is used to restore volume in the cheeks and midface, to soften nasolabial folds and cheek wrinkles, and, in its original indication, to correct facial lipoatrophy in HIV [1][3].

Unlike conventional hyaluronic acid fillers, PLLA is described as a biostimulator: its microparticles are said to provoke a controlled subclinical inflammatory response that lays down collagen, so results emerge over weeks to months and typically involve several treatment sessions [2][1]. Systematic reviews of randomized trials report improvements in skin quality, volume and lipoatrophy scores, with benefits sustained up to 25 months, and adverse events that are mostly mild to moderate [4][3].
In looksmaxxing communities, it is discussed mainly as an option for a gaunt face after weight loss; the community material is limited to a few forum questions [5].

paras: PLLA is a polymer of L-lactic acid. Grokipedia describes it as degrading by hydrolysis into lactic acid over roughly 6 to 24 months and being metabolised, with solid irregular particles in the 40 to 63 micron range [1]. A 2018 review states that the size and chemistry of the microparticles are central to the subclinical inflammatory response that stimulates collagen deposition and that this differentiates PLLA from other treatments [2].

Because it works by biostimulation, treatment typically involves several sessions spaced weeks apart, followed by maintenance, according to Grokipedia [1]. The wiki does not reproduce preparation or injection technique.

Systematic reviews. A 2024 systematic review in Polymers included 11 randomized trials in adults with facial aging or lipoatrophy; four showed increased dermal thickness and improved lipoatrophy and aesthetic scores, with effects sustained for at least 25 months, two showed superiority over injectable human collagen, and three favoured PLLA over a hyaluronic gel for lipoatrophy severity, skin quality, elasticity and satisfaction [3]. A 2026 systematic review of 14 studies of PLLA and calcium hydroxylapatite found improvements in elasticity, wrinkles and facial volume, with PLLA effects lasting up to 25 months versus 12 to 18 months for calcium hydroxylapatite [4].

Individual randomized trials. A randomized trial of Sculptra for cheek wrinkles compared it with no treatment in adults over 21 with moderate or severe wrinkles [6]. A split-face, double-blind non-inferiority trial compared a new PLLA filler (Gana V) with Sculptra in nasolabial folds [7]. A 2025 multicenter, evaluator-blinded superiority trial studied PLLA for midfacial volume loss and contour defects [8]. Randomized trials have also tested PLLA with microneedling radiofrequency for skin laxity and with fractional CO2 laser for acne scars [9][10].

Registered studies. Trials of Sculptra for midface volume deficit (205 participants) and nasolabial folds (80 participants) are registered as completed [11][12]. Smaller studies cover temple volume loss, cellulite of the buttocks and thighs, and histological changes in women at different menopausal stages [13][14][15]. A phase 2 study of PLLA in people using GLP-1 drugs, who may experience facial laxity, is registered but not yet recruiting [16].
Limits. The 2026 reviewers assessed risk of bias with the ROB2 tool, and a 2024 review notes that studies vary in design and comparators [4][3].

Across randomized trials the main adverse events were bruising, hematoma, tenderness, nodules and edema, all mild to moderate in intensity [3]. The 2026 systematic review lists pain and swelling at the injection site as the most frequent effects and describes at least one serious case [4]. Grokipedia states contraindications include hypersensitivity to components, active skin infection and a history of keloid scarring [1].

According to Grokipedia, the FDA approved Sculptra on 3 August 2004 for restoring and correcting facial fat loss in immune-competent people with HIV, extended its labelling to nasolabial folds in 2009, and added cheek wrinkles in 2023 [1]. Galderma is the manufacturer [1].

The only community material reviewed is a single looksmax.org thread in which a user with a gaunt face when losing weight asks for opinions on Sculptra, planning treatment within weeks [5]. No replies were available.

lore.intro: Community discussion of Sculptra is sparse; the main thread concerns using it for a hollow face after weight loss [5].
